claim: Long-term experimental evolution of Saccharomyces cerevisiae in ammonium-limited chemostats results in repeated selection for non-synonymous variation in the DNA binding domain of GAT1.
source: We studied adaptive evolution of gene expression using long-term experimental evolution of Saccharomyces cerevisiae in ammonium-limited chemostats. We found repeated selection for non-synonymous variation in the DNA binding domain of the transcriptional activator, GAT1, which functions with the repressor, DAL80 in an incoherent type-1 feedforward loop (I1-FFL) to control expression of the high affinity ammonium transporter gene, MEP2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from long-term experimental evolution experiments and whole genome sequencing showing recurrent GAT1 mutations.

claim: GAT1 functions with the repressor DAL80 in an incoherent type-1 feedforward loop (I1-FFL) to control expression of MEP2.
source: We found repeated selection for non-synonymous variation in the DNA binding domain of the transcriptional activator, GAT1, which functions with the repressor, DAL80 in an incoherent type-1 feedforward loop (I1-FFL) to control expression of the high affinity ammonium transporter gene, MEP2.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of the NCR regulatory network architecture and is supported by the experimental data in the study.

claim: Missense mutations in the DNA binding domain of GAT1 reduce its binding to the GATAA consensus sequence.
source: Missense mutations in the DNA binding domain of GAT1 reduce its binding to the GATAA consensus sequence.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSAs) showing reduced binding affinity.

claim: Decreases in GAT1 binding result in increased expression of MEP2 as a consequence of properties of I1-FFLs.
source: However, we show experimentally, and using mathematical modeling, that decreases in GAT1 binding result in increased expression of MEP2 as a consequence of properties of I1-FFLs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from GFP reporter assays and RNA-seq, as well as mathematical modeling of the I1-FFL.

claim: I1-FFLs can facilitate adaptive tuning of gene expression through modulation of transcription factor binding affinities.
source: Our results show that I1-FFLs, one of the most commonly occurring network motifs in transcriptional networks, can facilitate adaptive tuning of gene expression through modulation of transcription factor binding affinities.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing adaptive GAT1 mutations and their effects on gene expression, combined with inference about the general properties of I1-FFLs.

claim: Gene regulatory architectures are important in the evolution of gene expression.
source: Our findings highlight the importance of gene regulatory architectures in the evolution of gene expression.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings showing how the I1-FFL architecture enables adaptive evolution.

claim: Gene expression evolution is a pervasive source of phenotypic diversity between and within species.
source: Gene expression evolution is a pervasive source of phenotypic diversity between and within species (Jacob and Monod, 1961; Jacob, 1977; Nocedal and Johnson, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Incoherent type-1 feed-forward loops (I1-FFL) are one of the most common network motifs, occurring hundreds of times in bacteria and yeast gene regulatory networks.
source: Of these variants, incoherent type-1 feed-forward loops (I1-FFL) are one of the most common, occurring hundreds of times in bacteria and yeast gene regulatory networks (Lee et al., 2002; Mangan and Alon, 2003; Milo et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies that characterized network motifs in gene regulatory networks.

claim: I1-FFLs function to speed the response time of gene expression.
source: I1-FFL function to speed the response time of gene expression (Mangan and Alon, 2003) and for particular parameter values, detect relative changes in input signals rather than absolute levels of inputs (Goentoro et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies on I1-FFL dynamics.

claim: For particular parameter values, I1-FFLs detect relative changes in input signals rather than absolute levels of inputs.
source: I1-FFL function to speed the response time of gene expression (Mangan and Alon, 2003) and for particular parameter values, detect relative changes in input signals rather than absolute levels of inputs (Goentoro et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on I1-FFL behavior.

claim: Parallel changes in gene expression have been observed in replicated populations of both E. coli and S. cerevisiae during long-term experimental evolution.
source: LTEE in microorganisms provides evidence for the role of adaptive changes in gene expression in response to selection as parallel changes in gene expression have been observed in replicated populations of both E. coli (Cooper et al., 2003) and S. cerevisiae (Ferea et al., 1999; Gresham et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior LTEE studies.

claim: Copy number variants (CNVs) comprising gene amplifications that result in increased expression of transporter genes are a recurrent class of adaptive alleles in chemostat LTEE.
source: Copy number variants (CNVs), comprising gene amplifications that result in increased expression of transporter genes (Gresham et al., 2008; Hong and Gresham, 2014), are a recurrent class of adaptive alleles in chemostat LTEE.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies and is consistent with the data presented in this study.

claim: The regulation of nitrogen utilization in budding yeast is controlled by four transcription factors that bind to the same GATAA consensus sequence.
source: Control of nitrogen catabolite repression (NCR) transcription is achieved by four transcription factors, that bind to the same GATAA consensus sequence (Cooper, 2002; Magasanik and Kaiser, 2002; Hofman-Bang, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on NCR regulation.

claim: GLN3 and GAT1 have activating activity in NCR regulation.
source: Two factors – GLN3 and GAT1 – have activating activity and two factors – DAL80 and GZF3 – have repressive activity.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of NCR regulation cited in the manuscript.

claim: DAL80 and GZF3 have repressive activity in NCR regulation.
source: Two factors – GLN3 and GAT1 – have activating activity and two factors – DAL80 and GZF3 – have repressive activity.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of NCR regulation cited in the manuscript.

claim: GLN3 is constitutively expressed and regulated post-translationally by TORC1-dependent phosphorylation that prevents its entry into the nucleus.
source: GLN3 is constitutively expressed and regulated post-translationally by TORC1-dependent phosphorylation that prevents its entry into the nucleus.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of NCR regulation.

claim: In conditions in which TORC1 activity is low, dephosphorylation of GLN3 enables it to enter the nucleus where it activates expression of GAT1, DAL80 and GZF3.
source: In conditions in which TORC1 activity is low, dephosphorylation of GLN3 enables it to enter the nucleus where it activates expression of GAT1, DAL80 and GZF3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of NCR regulation and is illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The NCR regulatory components comprise four interconnected I1-FFLs that function to regulate the expression dynamics and output of ~41 target genes.
source: The NCR regulatory components comprise four interconnected I1-FFLs comprising either of the activators, GLN3 and GAT1, and either of the repressors DAL80 or GZF3, that function to regulate the expression dynamics and output of ~41 target genes (Godard et al., 2007) that encode products required for assimilating diverse nitrogen sources.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on NCR regulation.

claim: Evolution is highly parallel both at the phenotypic and genotypic levels over 250 generations in ammonium-limited chemostats.
source: We found that evolution is highly parallel both at the phenotypic and genotypic levels over 250 generations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from replicated LTEE experiments showing similar fitness trajectories and recurrent mutations.

claim: Significant increases in population level fitness were observed with an overall deceleration in the rate of fitness improvement with time.
source: We observed significant increases in population level fitness with an overall deceleration in the rate of fitness improvement with time as seen in previous LTEEs (Barrick et al., 2009) (Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from competitive fitness assays shown in Figure 1b and is consistent with prior LTEE studies.

claim: Recurrent selection for missense mutations in the DNA binding domain of GAT1 occurs during the early stages of adaptive evolution in each population.
source: Using whole genome, whole population sequencing of evolving populations, we identified recurrent selection for missense mutations in the DNA binding domain of GAT1 during the early stages of adaptive evolution in each population.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole genome sequencing data from the LTEE populations.

claim: CNVs that include MEP2 are identified at high frequencies following 250 generations of selection in ammonium-limited chemostats.
source: Consistent with positive selection for increased ammonium transport capacity in this environment, we also identified CNVs that include MEP2, which encodes a high-affinity ammonium transporter, at high frequencies following 250 generations of selection (Figure 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data and qPCR analysis shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Each of the evolving populations contained multiple different GAT1 mutations at frequencies of 10−2-10−3.
source: Each of the evolving populations contained multiple different GAT1 mutations at frequencies of 10−2-10−3.
evidence: This claim is supported by targeted deep sequencing data.

claim: GAT1 alleles reach their highest frequencies during the early stages of adaptive evolution before lineages containing MEP2 CNVs ultimately rise to high frequency in each population.
source: These GAT1 alleles reach their highest frequencies during the early stages of adaptive evolution before lineages containing MEP2 CNVs ultimately rise to high frequency in each population.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data tracking allele frequencies over time.

claim: All identified GAT1 mutations are missense mutations in its DNA binding domain.
source: Importantly, all identified GAT1 mutations are missense mutations in its DNA binding domain (Figure 1e), which we find is under strong purifying selection in natural environments (Figure 1f).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The DNA binding domain of GAT1 is under strong purifying selection in natural environments.
source: Importantly, all identified GAT1 mutations are missense mutations in its DNA binding domain (Figure 1e), which we find is under strong purifying selection in natural environments (Figure 1f).
evidence: This claim is supported by dN/dS analysis of GAT1 sequences from wild yeast strains shown in Figure 1f.

claim: All strains containing GAT1 missense mutations are significantly increased in fitness in ammonium-limited chemostats.
source: All strains containing GAT1 missense mutations are significantly increased in fitness in ammonium-limited chemostats, but exhibit decreased fitness in all other nitrogen-limited conditions consistent with antagonistic pleiotropy (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by competitive fitness assay data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: GAT1 missense mutations exhibit decreased fitness in all other nitrogen-limited conditions (glutamine, proline, urea) consistent with antagonistic pleiotropy.
source: All strains containing GAT1 missense mutations are significantly increased in fitness in ammonium-limited chemostats, but exhibit decreased fitness in all other nitrogen-limited conditions consistent with antagonistic pleiotropy (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by competitive fitness assay data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: A GAT1 knock out (KO) strain exhibits a fitness defect in both ammonium and proline limited chemostats.
source: By contrast, a GAT1 knock out (KO) strain exhibits a fitness defect in both ammonium and proline limited chemostats.
evidence: This claim is supported by competitive fitness assay data.

claim: GAT1 mutations are nearly neutral in YPD batch media conditions in which GAT1 and the entire NCR regulon is transcriptionally repressed.
source: GAT1 mutations are nearly neutral in YPD batch media conditions in which GAT1, and the entire NCR regulon, is transcriptionally repressed.
evidence: This claim is supported by competitive fitness assay data and is consistent with knowledge of NCR regulation.

claim: Missense mutations in the DNA binding domain of GAT1 acquired during LTEE alter its function rather than rendering it non-functional.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that missense mutations in the DNA binding domain of GAT1 acquired during LTEE alter its function rather than rendering it non-functional.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the fitness data showing that GAT1 mutations have different effects than GAT1 knockout.

claim: Deletion of MEP2 ORF and its promoter sequences is highly deleterious in ammonium-limited chemostats regardless of the genotype of GAT1.
source: All strains had severely reduced fitness (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a) consistent with the beneficial effect of GAT1 variants being dependent, at least in part, on MEP2 expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by competitive fitness assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The beneficial effect of GAT1 variants is dependent, at least in part, on MEP2 expression.
source: All strains had severely reduced fitness (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a) consistent with the beneficial effect of GAT1 variants being dependent, at least in part, on MEP2 expression.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the fitness data of MEP2 deletion strains.

claim: Increased copy number of MEP2 correlates with increased mRNA expression.
source: Increased copy number of MEP2 correlates with increased mRNA expression and results in fitness increases (s > 1.3) greater than that conferred by GAT1 variants (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Increased copy number of MEP2 results in fitness increases (s > 1.3) greater than that conferred by GAT1 variants.
source: Increased copy number of MEP2 correlates with increased mRNA expression and results in fitness increases (s > 1.3) greater than that conferred by GAT1 variants (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by competitive fitness assay data comparing MEP2 CNV strains to GAT1 variant strains.

claim: GAT1 mutations result in increased expression of genes encoding ammonium transporters (MEP1, MEP2, and MEP3).
source: GAT1 mutations result in increased expression of genes encoding ammonium transporters (MEP1, MEP2, and MEP3) as well as transporters that import other nitrogen sources such as urea, allantoin and GABA.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: GAT1 mutations result in increased expression of transporters that import other nitrogen sources such as urea, allantoin and GABA.
source: GAT1 mutations result in increased expression of genes encoding ammonium transporters (MEP1, MEP2, and MEP3) as well as transporters that import other nitrogen sources such as urea, allantoin and GABA.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: GAT1 mutations result in a strong reduction in DAL80 expression.
source: By contrast, GAT1 mutations result in a strong reduction in DAL80 expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: The expression of GLN3 and GZF3 is unchanged in the presence of GAT1 variants.
source: The expression of GLN3 and GZF3 is unchanged in the presence of GAT1 variants (Supplementary file 1B) suggesting that the altered expression of MEP2 and DAL80 is attributable to changes in GAT1 binding affinity.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: The altered expression of MEP2 and DAL80 in GAT1 variant strains is attributable to changes in GAT1 binding affinity.
source: The expression of GLN3 and GZF3 is unchanged in the presence of GAT1 variants (Supplementary file 1B) suggesting that the altered expression of MEP2 and DAL80 is attributable to changes in GAT1 binding affinity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the RNA-seq data showing unchanged GLN3 and GZF3 expression.

claim: GAT1 variants result in increased expression of GAT1 itself.
source: Interestingly, GAT1 variants also result in increased expression of GAT1 itself.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: All adaptive GAT1 mutations result in strongly reduced DAL80 expression and increased MEP2 expression compared to the wild type.
source: All adaptive GAT1 mutations result in strongly reduced DAL80 expression and increased MEP2 expression compared to the wild type, while a GAT1 KO strain showed slightly reduced DAL80 expression and decreased MEP2 expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by GFP reporter assay data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: A GAT1 KO strain showed slightly reduced DAL80 expression and decreased MEP2 expression.
source: All adaptive GAT1 mutations result in strongly reduced DAL80 expression and increased MEP2 expression compared to the wild type, while a GAT1 KO strain showed slightly reduced DAL80 expression and decreased MEP2 expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by GFP reporter assay data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: DAL80 and MEP2 promoter activities in heterozygous diploids (gat1-1/GAT1) were identical to the haploid ancestral strain containing a wildtype GAT1 allele.
source: DAL80 and MEP2 promoter activities in these heterozygotes were identical to the haploid ancestral strain (FY4) containing a wildtype GAT1 allele indicating that the missense mutations of GAT1 are recessive and therefore unlikely to have gain-of-function or dominant negative effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by GFP reporter assay data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The missense mutations of GAT1 are recessive and therefore unlikely to have gain-of-function or dominant negative effects.
source: DAL80 and MEP2 promoter activities in these heterozygotes were identical to the haploid ancestral strain (FY4) containing a wildtype GAT1 allele indicating that the missense mutations of GAT1 are recessive and therefore unlikely to have gain-of-function or dominant negative effects.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the GFP reporter assay data in heterozygous diploids.

claim: The maintenance, but reduced, expression of DAL80 and MEP2 in the GAT1 KO background is due to the activity of GLN3.
source: The maintenance, but reduced, expression of DAL80 and MEP2 in the GAT1 KO background (Figure 3b) is due to the activity of GLN3 as a gat1 gln3 double KO results in no expression from the DAL80 and MEP2 promoters (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by GFP reporter assay data in double knockout strains shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: GLN3 is required for expression of MEP2 in the presence of GAT1 variants.
source: GLN3 is required for expression of MEP2 in the presence of GAT1 variants (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), likely due to its role in activating the entire NCR regulon, but in these strains the expression of GLN3 is not increased and therefore does not contribute to the increased steady-state expression of MEP2.
evidence: This claim is supported by GFP reporter assay data in gat1 gln3 double knockout strains.

claim: The expression of GLN3 is not increased in GAT1 variant strains and therefore does not contribute to the increased steady-state expression of MEP2.
source: GLN3 is required for expression of MEP2 in the presence of GAT1 variants (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), likely due to its role in activating the entire NCR regulon, but in these strains the expression of GLN3 is not increased and therefore does not contribute to the increased steady-state expression of MEP2.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from RNA-seq data showing unchanged GLN3 expression.

claim: Adaptive GAT1 alleles failed to show evidence for any significant binding specificity using protein binding microarrays (PBMs).
source: Whereas the ancestral GAT1 DNA binding domain shows clear evidence of specificity for the GATAA consensus sequence, adaptive GAT1 alleles failed to show evidence for any significant binding specificity using PBMs (Supplementary file 2A) indicating that their functional and fitness effects are not exerted by the acquisition of new DNA binding specificities.
evidence: This claim is supported by protein binding microarray data.

claim: The functional and fitness effects of adaptive GAT1 alleles are not exerted by the acquisition of new DNA binding specificities.
source: Whereas the ancestral GAT1 DNA binding domain shows clear evidence of specificity for the GATAA consensus sequence, adaptive GAT1 alleles failed to show evidence for any significant binding specificity using PBMs (Supplementary file 2A) indicating that their functional and fitness effects are not exerted by the acquisition of new DNA binding specificities.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the PBM data showing loss of binding specificity.

claim: Adaptive GAT1 variants showed significantly decreased binding affinity to all target motifs in MEP2 and DAL80 promoters.
source: Adaptive GAT1 variants showed significantly decreased binding affinity to all target motifs (Figure 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Adaptive GAT1 mutations have a more detrimental effect on binding to the DAL80 promoter GATAA site compared with the two MEP2 promoter binding sites.
source: Binding kinetics calculated based on a two parameter Michaelis-Menten model (Stormo and Zhao, 2010) show that adaptive GAT1 mutations have a more detrimental effect on binding to the DAL80 promoter GATAA site compared with the two MEP2 promoter binding sites likely reflecting differences in motif strength (Figure 4c and Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of EMSA data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The differential effect of GAT1 variants on DAL80 and MEP2 promoters likely reflects differences in motif strength.
source: Binding kinetics calculated based on a two parameter Michaelis-Menten model (Stormo and Zhao, 2010) show that adaptive GAT1 mutations have a more detrimental effect on binding to the DAL80 promoter GATAA site compared with the two MEP2 promoter binding sites likely reflecting differences in motif strength (Figure 4c and Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the EMSA data and knowledge of promoter motif strength.

claim: The adaptive GAT1 alleles encode functional TFs that maintain sequence specificity for GATAA binding sites, but exhibit a quantitative decrease in affinity for their target sites compared to the ancestral allele.
source: This suggests that the adaptive GAT1 alleles encode functional TFs that maintain sequence specificity for GATAA binding sites, but exhibit a quantitative decrease in affinity for their target sites compared to the ancestral allele.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the EMSA and PBM data.

claim: There is a significant positive correlation between gene expression levels of NCR genes and the estimated affinity of each promoter for GAT1.
source: Consistent with a differential effect of reduced GAT1 binding affinity on different promoters, we identified a significant positive correlation between gene expression levels of NCR genes and the estimated affinity of each promoter for GAT1 (Figure 4d).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of RNA-seq data and promoter affinity scores shown in Figure 4d.

claim: A net increase in MEP2 expression results when decreased activation at the DAL80 promoter is the only functional effect of GAT1 variation.
source: Using a mathematical model of I1-FFLs we confirmed that a net increase in MEP2 expression results when decreased activation at the DAL80 promoter is the only functional effect of GAT1 variation (Figure 4f).
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modeling results shown in Figure 4f.

claim: A GAT1 variant that results in a decrease in direct activation of the MEP2 promoter will result in increased expression of MEP2 when activation of the DAL80 promoter is also decreased.
source: However, using this model we also find that a GAT1 variant that results in a decrease in direct activation of the MEP2 promoter will result in increased expression of MEP2 when activation of the DAL80 promoter is also decreased.
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modeling results.

claim: Increased MEP2 expression, despite decreased activation of the MEP2 promoter, is enhanced by a greater relative decrease in DAL80 activation.
source: Increased MEP2 expression, despite decreased activation of the MEP2 promoter, is enhanced by a greater relative decrease in DAL80 activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modeling results.

claim: Decreased binding affinity of GAT1, leading to decreased activation of both the DAL80 and MEP2 promoters, can simultaneously result in decreased expression of the repressor DAL80 and increased expression of the target gene MEP2.
source: Thus, our model of a I1-FFL is consistent with the finding that decreased binding affinity of GAT1, leading to decreased activation of both the DAL80 and MEP2 promoters (Figure 4b and Figure 4c) can simultaneously result in decreased expression of the repressor, DAL80 and increased expression of the target gene, MEP2 (Figure 3a and Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by integration of experimental data (EMSA, RNA-seq, GFP reporter assays) and mathematical modeling.

claim: Increased expression of GAT1 in GAT1 variant strains is likely due to the same phenomenon that results in increased MEP2 expression.
source: As GAT1 activates its own expression and is also repressed by DAL80, increased expression of GAT1 is likely due to the same phenomenon that results in increased MEP2 expression.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the RNA-seq data and knowledge of GAT1 auto-regulation.

claim: The increase in GAT1 expression likely also contributes to increased MEP2 expression.
source: The increase in GAT1 expression likely also contributes to increased MEP2 expression, as modeling an increase in GAT1 expression results in increased MEP2 expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on inference supported by mathematical modeling shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Missense mutations in GAT1 are under strong positive selection in populations evolving in a constant ammonium-limited environment.
source: We find that missense mutations in GAT1 are under strong positive selection in populations evolving in a constant ammonium-limited environment.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data showing recurrent GAT1 mutations and their dynamics in evolving populations.

claim: The functional effects of adaptive GAT1 mutations are the result of increasing the output from an I1-FFL by reducing the binding affinity of the activator, GAT1.
source: The functional effects of adaptive GAT1 mutations are the result of increasing the output from an I1-FFL, one of the most frequently occurring network motifs in transcriptional networks, by reducing the binding affinity of the activator, GAT1.
evidence: This claim is supported by integration of experimental data (EMSA, RNA-seq, GFP reporter assays) and mathematical modeling.

claim: The functional effect of adaptive GAT1 variation is mediated by increased expression of a high affinity ammonium transporter that results in increased fitness in the ammonium-limited environment.
source: The functional effect of adaptive GAT1 variation is mediated by increased expression of a high affinity ammonium transporter that results in increased fitness in the ammonium-limited environment.
evidence: This claim is supported by integration of gene expression data, fitness assays, and MEP2 deletion experiments.

claim: Targeted deep sequencing of evolving populations identified many GAT1 mutations that are under positive selection but never increase to population frequencies greater than 1%.
source: Consistent with this observation, we find that targeted deep sequencing of evolving populations identified many GAT1 mutations in evolving populations that are under positive selection, but never increase to population frequencies greater than 1%.
evidence: This claim is supported by targeted deep sequencing data.

claim: Beneficial mutations that do not persist in the population are not detected by population-level sequencing.
source: These beneficial mutations are not detected by population-level sequencing.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from comparing whole genome sequencing and targeted deep sequencing results.

claim: Decreasing the binding affinity of GAT1 for its target sequence increases expression output from the MEP2 promoter as well as other GAT1 targets with strong promoters.
source: Here, we have shown that decreasing the binding affinity of GAT1 for its target sequence increases expression output from the MEP2 promoter as well as other GAT1 targets with strong promoters.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and GFP reporter assay data.

claim: The increase in MEP2 expression is attributed to decreased affinity of GAT1 for its consensus sequence, which reduces transcriptional output from the DAL80 promoter.
source: We attribute the increase in MEP2 expression to decreased affinity of GAT1 for its consensus sequence, which reduces transcriptional output from the DAL80 promoter, a comparatively weak promoter.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from EMSA data and gene expression data.

claim: A reduction in the effective concentration of the repressor DAL80 results in increased transcriptional output from the MEP2 promoter.
source: A reduction in the effective concentration of the repressor results in increased transcriptional output from the MEP2 promoter.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the I1-FFL architecture and experimental data.

claim: A proportionally greater decrease in DAL80 expression can outweigh the effect of reduced activation of the MEP2 promoter.
source: However, as illustrated by our model (Figure 4f), a proportionally greater decrease in DAL80 expression can outweigh the effect of reduced activation of the MEP2 promoter.
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modeling shown in Figure 4f.

claim: GAT1 is auto-regulatory.
source: GAT1 is auto-regulatory and we observe that GAT1 variants also result in increased GAT1 expression, which further increases expression output from the MEP2 promoter (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of GAT1 regulation and is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Increased GAT1 expression in GAT1 variant strains further increases expression output from the MEP2 promoter.
source: GAT1 is auto-regulatory and we observe that GAT1 variants also result in increased GAT1 expression, which further increases expression output from the MEP2 promoter (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from RNA-seq data and mathematical modeling shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Remodeling the GAT1-DAL80-MEP2 I1-FFL is a frequently occurring repeatable mode of adaptive evolution during the earliest stages of adaptive evolution in ammonium-limited environments.
source: The preponderance of these mutations within and between populations suggests that remodeling the GAT1-DAL80-MEP2 I1-FFL is a frequently occurring repeatable mode of adaptive evolution during the earliest stages of adaptive evolution in ammonium-limited environments.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the sequencing data showing recurrent GAT1 mutations across replicate populations.

claim: Adaptive GAT1 alleles likely do not represent a fitness optimum in the ammonium-limited environment.
source: However, adaptive GAT1 alleles likely do not represent a fitness optimum in the ammonium-limited environment as, in contrast to our previous study (Hong and Gresham, 2014), we found that ultimately these alleles were outcompeted by lineages containing MEP2 amplifications.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the allele frequency dynamics showing GAT1 mutations being replaced by MEP2 CNVs.

claim: MEP2 amplifications have the same functional effect as adaptive GAT1 mutations: they increase expression of MEP2 enabling improved ammonium transport capabilities.
source: MEP2 amplifications have the same functional effect as adaptive GAT1 mutations: they increase expression of MEP2 enabling improved ammonium transport capabilities.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the gene expression and fitness data for both types of mutations.

claim: The increased expression of other high affinity transporters in GAT1 lineages that are unable to transport ammonium may confer a fitness cost that is not associated with MEP2 amplification alleles.
source: However, the increased expression of other high affinity transporters in GAT1 lineages that are unable to transport ammonium may confer a fitness cost that is not associated with MEP2 amplification alleles.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the RNA-seq data showing broad upregulation of NCR genes in GAT1 variant strains.

claim: The evolutionary hotspot in the DNA binding domain of GAT1 is reminiscent of hotspots in transcriptional regulators important in tumorigenesis including recurrent missense mutations in the DNA binding domain of TP53 and CTCF.
source: The evolutionary hotspot in the DNA binding domain of GAT1 identified in this study is reminiscent of hotspots in transcriptional regulators important in tumorigenesis including recurrent missense mutations in the DNA binding domain of TP53, a driver in the majority of human cancers (Freed-Pastor and Prives, 2012), and CTCF, a poly-zinc finger transcription factor regulating oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes (Ong and Corces, 2014).
evidence: This claim draws an analogy to cancer biology based on citations to prior literature.

claim: Missense mutations in the DNA binding domain of TP53 and CTCF result in altered binding affinities at the promoters of target genes resulting in aberrant transcriptional activation in various cancers.
source: As with adaptive evolution, missense mutations in the DNA binding domain of these transcription factors result in altered binding affinities at the promoters of target genes resulting in aberrant transcriptional activation in various cancers (Park et al., 1994; Inga et al., 2001; Filippova et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior cancer biology literature.

claim: I1-FFLs may serve a general evolutionary role as facilitators of transcriptional tuning through modulation of transcriptional factor binding affinities.
source: As I1-FFL are one of the most frequent motifs in transcriptional networks they may serve a general evolutionary role as facilitators of transcriptional tuning through modulation of transcriptional factor binding affinities.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental findings and knowledge of I1-FFL prevalence.

claim: The ancestral strain used for all LTEE is a prototrophic haploid derivative (FY4; MATa) of the S288c reference strain.
source: The ancestral strain used for all LTEE is a prototrophic haploid derivative (FY4; MATa) of the S288c reference strain.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the experimental materials.

claim: Three chemostat vessels were founded with a clonal ancestral population and maintained under constant dilution with defined media containing 0.4 mM (NH4)2SO4 (0.8mM nitrogen).
source: Three chemostat vessels w ere founded with a clonal ancestral population and maintained under constant dilution with defined media containing 0.4 mM (NH 4) 2 SO 4 , (0.8mM nitrogen).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the experimental design shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Chemostats were maintained in continuous mode for 250 generations (~3 months).
source: Chemostats were maintained in continuous mode for 250 generations (~ 3 months) and samples obtained every 10-20 generations for archiving.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the experimental design.

claim: The rate of fitness improvement decelerates over time for three independently replicated LTEE.
source: The rate of fitness improvement decelerates over time for three independently replicated LTEE (R1, R2 and R3).
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness assay data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: GAT1 variants are a primary target in the earliest generations of selection but, in some LTEE, are ultimately replaced by other alleles including CNVs that encompass MEP2.
source: GAT1 (red lines) variants are a primary target in the earliest generations of selection but, in some LTEE, are ultimately replaced by other alleles including CNVs that encompass MEP2 (blue lines) and mutations in genes that control cell cycle and growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data tracking allele frequencies shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Multiple missense mutations in GAT1 are present simultaneously in each population and compete with each other during the earliest generations.
source: Multiple missense mutations in GAT1 are present simultaneously in each population and compete with each other during the earliest generations.
evidence: This claim is supported by targeted deep sequencing data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The DNA binding domain of GAT1 is a mutational hotspot in all ammonium-limited LTEE.
source: The DNA binding domain of GAT1 is a mutational hotspot in all ammonium-limited LTEE.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data showing the distribution of mutations shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Multiple missense (protein coding alteration) mutations were observed in GAT1 but no nonsense or frame-shift mutations were detected.
source: Multiple missense (protein coding alteration) mutations were observed but no nonsense or frame-shift mutations were detected.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Unlike LTEE in ammonium-limited chemostats, the GAT1 DNA binding domain is under purifying selection in wild yeast strains.
source: Unlike LTEE in ammonium-limited chemostats, the GAT1 DNA binding domain is under purifying selection implying that non-synonymous mutations are likely to be detrimental in dynamic environments.
evidence: This claim is supported by dN/dS analysis shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Non-synonymous mutations in the GAT1 DNA binding domain are likely to be detrimental in dynamic environments.
source: Unlike LTEE in ammonium-limited chemostats, the GAT1 DNA binding domain is under purifying selection implying that non-synonymous mutations are likely to be detrimental in dynamic environments.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the dN/dS analysis showing purifying selection in natural populations.

claim: Under nitrogen rich conditions, GLN3 and any GAT1 are phosphorylated and retained in the cytoplasm in a TORC1-dependent manner.
source: Under nitrogen rich conditions, GLN3, and any GAT1, are phosphorylated and retained in the cytoplasm in a TORC1-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of NCR regulation illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In nitrogen-poor conditions, GLN3 and GAT1 are dephosphorylated allowing them to enter the nucleus and activate NCR sensitive genes.
source: In nitrogen-poor conditions, GLN3 and GAT1 are dephosphorylated allowing them to enter the nucleus and activate NCR sensitive genes.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of NCR regulation illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The activator GLN3 is constitutively expressed and acts to initiate NCR expression subject to post-translational regulation.
source: The activator GLN3 is constitutively expressed and acts to initiate NCR expression subject to post-translational regulation.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of NCR regulation illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: GFP expression levels measured using the reporter assay were highly comparable to RNA-seq data.
source: GFP expression levels measured using this assay were highly comparable to RNA-seq data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b) and therefore a good proxy of transcriptional activation of each promoter in the background of the different GAT1 variants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b and 1c.

claim: MEP2 contains two distinct GATAA sequence motifs in its promoter region whereas DAL80 possesses only one.
source: MEP2 contains two distinct GATAA sequence motifs in its promoter region whereas DAL80 possesses only one.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis of the promoter regions.

claim: GAT1-1 (W321L) shows a much stronger reduction in DNA binding affinity compared to GAT1-3 (R345G) for both tested promoter sequences.
source: Interestingly, GAT1-1 (W321L) shows a much stronger reduction in DNA binding affinity compared to GAT1-3 (R345G) for both tested promoter sequences (Figure 4b and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 4b and 4c.

claim: The residue (R345) altered in the GAT1-3 allele is the most frequently mutated site in multiple LTEEs whereas only a single variant was identified at the site mutated in the GAT1-1 allele (W321).
source: First, we find that the residue (R345) altered in the GAT1-3 allele is the most frequently mutated site in multiple LTEEs whereas only a single variant was identified at the site mutated in the GAT1-1 allele (W321) (Figure 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The GAT1-3 variant results in higher relative fitness compared to the GAT1-1 variant.
source: Second, the GAT1-3 variant results in higher relative fitness compared to the GAT1-1 variant (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by competitive fitness assay data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Intermediate reductions in GAT1 binding affinity may be more beneficial than strongly reduced binding.
source: These observations suggest that intermediate reductions in GAT1 binding affinity may be more beneficial than strongly reduced binding.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the fitness and binding affinity data.

claim: Complete loss of GAT1 results in decreased MEP2 expression and is deleterious.
source: Consistent with this claim, complete loss of GAT1 results in decreased MEP2 expression (Figure 3b) and is deleterious (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by GFP reporter assay data and fitness assay data shown in Figures 3b and 2b.
